title: Two live meanings of the rule of law

body: The United Nations describes the rule of law as a principle of governance in which all persons, institutions, and entities, public and private, including the state itself, are accountable to laws that are publicly promulgated, equally enforced, and independently adjudicated, and that are consistent with international human rights norms and standards. That definition builds human rights into the idea. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry on the rule of law records a different insistence. Joseph Raz, in particular, argues that the rule of law should be distinguished from democracy, human rights, and social justice, or the phrase stops identifying anything of its own. Both uses are current. One folds several political ideals together. The other tries to keep a thinner ideal: laws that are prospective, public, and capable of being followed, applied by accessible courts. This card does not pick a definition. Using the phrase as if it had only one meaning hides the disagreement.
